title: Circular Data First Decisions
notes: Open the lecture by slowing down the word angle. The chapter is not merely about plotting numbers on a circle. It asks what kind of observation produced the angle, which conventions made the coordinate label, and which displays preserve the geometry of that sample space.

title: Route Through The Chapter
notes: Use the route as a compact map of the assigned span. The notebook starts with coordinate conventions, then tests displays on one sample, then handles axial observations, and finally separates two generative mechanisms: wrapping a line and projecting a vector.

title: The Observation Is Not The Label
notes: Emphasize that the point on the circle is the observation and the numerical angle is a coordinate label. Moving the zero direction or changing orientation relabels the same geometry, while confusing the observation type changes the problem itself.

title: Clock And Compass Conventions
notes: Compare the two convention panels carefully. Clock data usually wrap a line with a chosen period, while compass bearings often use north as zero and measure clockwise. Both can be stored as angles, but their signs, cut points, and scientific questions differ.

title: Four Honest Displays
notes: Frame the display slide as a design problem. A raw circular plot avoids bins, a circular histogram groups counts around the circle, a rose diagram must encode counts by area, and an unrolled histogram is only honest when the cut point is declared.

title: Circular Bins Preserve The Sample
notes: The key invariant for a binned circular display is count preservation. Bins are arranged around the boundary so that a cluster crossing zero degrees is still adjacent to itself. Ask students to inspect whether the boundary is treated as a seam or as a neighbor relation.

title: Rose Area Carries Frequency
notes: Use this slide to prevent the most common rose diagram mistake. If the radius is proportional to frequency, area grows quadratically and large bins are exaggerated. To make sector area proportional to count, the radius should scale like the square root of the count.

title: The Cut Point Can Invent A Story
notes: The unrolled histogram is useful precisely because it reveals how much the conclusion depends on the chosen cut. A cluster near zero degrees becomes split when the cut passes through it, yet the same observations look unified when the cut is moved opposite the cluster.

title: Axial Observations Identify Opposites
notes: Make the distinction between directions and axes explicit. Directional data distinguish an arrow from its reverse, but axial data record an unoriented line. Treating an axis as a direction doubles the apparent categories and can make summaries point to a false preferred orientation.

title: Doubling Turns Axes Into Directions
notes: Explain doubling as a modeling map, not a cosmetic plotting trick. Because theta and theta plus pi represent the same axis, multiplying by two sends both representatives to the same circular direction modulo two pi. Interpretation then has to be halved back to axes.

title: Wrapping Starts From A Line
notes: For clock-like observations, begin with a linear variable and reduce it modulo a period. The cut point is arbitrary but visible, and periodic distance must cross the boundary correctly. The example distance from 23 to 1 hours is two hours, not twenty-two.

title: Projection Starts From A Vector
notes: For compass-like observations, the angle comes from projecting a nonzero planar vector to the unit circle. The unstable case is not a bad cut point but a vector near the origin, where the direction is poorly determined even before an angle is assigned.

title: A Pre-Statistics Decision Tree
notes: Present this as the checklist before computing any circular statistic. Decide whether the data wrap a period, project a direction, or identify antipodal axes. Then choose a display whose invariants match that observation type rather than retrofitting a linear plot afterward.

title: Invariant Checks
notes: The formulas are small because they are meant to be reused. Wrapping keeps values inside the period, projection returns unit vectors away from the origin, axial doubling identifies antipodes, and binned displays preserve the sample count. These checks make the visual argument auditable.

title: Carry Forward
notes: Close by connecting the opening chapter to the rest of directional statistics. Later chapters estimate mean direction, concentration, model fit, and regression, but all of that assumes the initial sample space was chosen correctly. Geometry is the first statistical assumption here.
